blocks.text: 概览

inlines.text: 概览
开发者日复一日地在同一批代码库中使用 AI 编程智能体，但智能体往往每次会话都从零开始：重新摸索熟悉的事实、加载用不上的工具、重复此前不成功的做法。
TokenEconomizer 是一款开源插件，它能从智能体在某个代码库中的历史会话中学习，减少后续会话中的浪费，而且无需改动智能体或其底层模型。
在 277 个真实的缺陷修复任务中，TokenEconomizer 让多个 AI 编程智能体的成本降低了 18.4%–30.9%。所有测试过的代码库成本都有下降，任务成功率则基本保持稳定。

blocks.text: AI 编程智能体正越来越多地帮助开发者基本独立地修复缺陷、构建功能，但每一次与模型的交互都会消耗 token。在每次会话中，智能体都要向模型发送指令、工具描述和会话历史。多数降低这部分成本的努力都聚焦于单个任务。然而开发者会反复回到同一批代码库，这就给了智能体从以往工作中学习的机会。缺少这种学习，智能体可能反复重新摸索如何运行测试、加载它从不使用的工具，或者花上几十轮反复纠缠同一个错误。

blocks.text: 在我们的论文 TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents 中，我们提出了一个简单的问题：在某个代码库中积累的经验，能否帮助智能体更高效地完成后续任务？TokenEconomizer 是来自加州大学伯克利分校、微软研究院和微软安全团队的开源插件，它把已完成的会话转化为对后续会话的指导。它降低浪费的同时不改动智能体或其底层模型，因此开发者可以把它与已经在用的编程智能体搭配使用。

blocks.text: 我们首先在 SWE-Bench 的 60 个任务上对 Claude Code 做了分析。SWE-Bench 是一个基于开源 Python 项目真实缺陷修复的基准测试，我们按顺序运行每个代码库的任务。有三类浪费反复出现：

inlines.text: 我们首先在 SWE-Bench 的 60 个任务上对 Claude Code 做了分析。SWE-Bench 是一个基于开源 Python 项目真实缺陷修复的基准测试，我们按顺序运行每个代码库的任务。有三类浪费反复出现：
反复重新摸索同样的事实
。当一个代码库累计完成至少五个任务后，30% 的工具调用重复了该代码库中更早任务里的某个操作。只有 7% 与另一个代码库历史中的操作相匹配。
为用不上的工具付费
。智能体每一轮都会收到 23 个工具描述，但其中 16 个从未被调用。
卡在失败上
。失败的任务占 17%，却消耗了 32% 的费用。

blocks.text: 我们还测试了三款流行的开源插件，它们各自围绕一种固定的省钱策略构建。每款插件都能降低部分代码库的成本，但在另一些代码库上则不然。综合来看，这些发现说明有效的成本控制必须因代码库而异，而不能到处套用同一种策略。

blocks.text: 微技能用一行式笔记记录代码库特有的知识。TokenEconomizer 会识别跨会话反复出现的模式，并提出相应的笔记。只有在多个会话确认该模式之后，笔记才会被加入智能体的起始上下文；如果后续证据与之矛盾，则会停用该笔记。

inlines.text: 未来展望

blocks.text: TokenEconomizer 为编码智能体开辟了一条新路径：不仅学会如何解决任务，还学会如何更有效地使用计算资源。其轻量级控制器展示了经验如何在不改变底层智能体或模型的情况下提升效率。

blocks.text: 这个开源插件让开发者和研究者都能接触这些方向。它的设计目标是与现有 AI 编码智能体并行运行，无需修改其底层模型，自身也不需要 API 密钥，并且学到的内容都保留在开发者本机。我们邀请社区以它为起点，探索那些能随经验变得更善于调配资源的智能体——既调整工作方式，也调整知识储备。

TokenEconomizer：从经验中学习，让 AI 编码智能体更高效
首发于

blocks.alt: Six coding sessions with shrinking cost bars send their logs to TokenEconomizer, which uses micro-skills, tool pruning and failure-loop intervention to guide an unchanged coding agent through the next session.

blocks.text: At a glance

inlines.text: At a glance

Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches.
TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model.

Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable.

blocks.text: AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session, an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error.

blocks.text: In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents, we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on.

blocks.text: We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred:

inlines.text: We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred:
Rediscovering the same facts

. After a repository had accumulated at least five completed tasks, 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository. Only 7% matched an action in another repository’s history.
Paying for unused tools
. The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called.
Getting stuck on failures
. The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of the spending.

blocks.text: We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere.

blocks.text: How TokenEconomizer works

inlines.text: How TokenEconomizer works

blocks.text: After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2.

inlines.text: After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2.

blocks.text: Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it.

inlines.text: Micro-skills

capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it.

blocks.text: Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use, while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed.

blocks.text: Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself.

Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction.

blocks.text: Looking ahead

inlines.text: Looking ahead

blocks.text: TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model.

inlines.text: TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model.

blocks.text: The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know.
